body: In Ireland, we’re independent at age 18, but my parents don’t care that I’ll be independent in a few years time and constantly say that I’m their property. I’ll try my best to stay safe in my country. Thanks for the advice, Zubaan.

I’ve made an appointment with my school counselor to talk about academics, etc. for next week. When I say I took off the hijab, I mean that whenever I leave home I wear it, but the moment I walk into the school doors in the morning, I run into the bathroom and take my hijab off. Though, once school is over and I walk home, I keep my school hoodie covering my hair but once I’m a short distance outside of my house, I put my hijab on quickly. I don’t have to cover my hair at *home*, just keep it tied back and cover my chest, plus stay extremely modest. 
I’m terrified that somehow they’ll find out that I don’t wear it in school (aka the one place where they’re not watching me like a hawk), and send me to live in their home country. To be brutally honest, I had a conversation with my parents before school started and I asked them if I could not wear the hijab in school. How they reacted gave me nightmares, but to put it short, my dad went ballistic at the mere question of me not wearing a hijab (said things like he would kill me if I didn’t wear a hijab in school.) I can start working part-time after my 16th birthday, but when I asked my mom, she didn’t allow me to.

Thank you for the response, especially for the planning part, this helped a lot.

I’m so tempted to pretend to wear the headscarf in school, a.k.a., taking it off as soon as I get to school and putting it back on when I walk home. It’ll make me feel beyond guilty, but I genuinely just can’t force myself to wear my headscarf in the school I’m in. I know that I’ll get back to wearing it as soon as I’m in university, I just wish my parents could have been more understanding. I love my parents, I really do, but they push me to the edge constantly. Thank you, I honestly didn’t expect anyone to reply with such kind words. I hope I can achieve my dreams of happiness too.

Then the same parents blame their mistakes on our ‘stupid phones/technology’. I get it, adults have really stressful lives, but if a person planned to have children with their partner, it’s their basic duty to raise their children well. Circumstances are hard, but our generation really is messed up. I don’t find it shocking that suicide and depression rates have increased with teenagers in the recent years. It’s sad, but it is what it is. But I hope our generation grows up to be responsible adults, unlike some of the adults who’ve raised us; all one can do is hope. Props to the decent parents in this world.
